title: Musculoskeletal Genetics
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how genes build bone, cartilage, and muscle, and how particular kinds of mutation produce particular diseases. It covers the transcription factors that direct skeletal development, the receptor gain of function behind achondroplasia, dominant negative collagen defects, the dystrophin reading frame, repeat expansion, mitochondrial inheritance, and the tumor suppressor and fusion gene changes that drive bone sarcomas. Board questions rarely ask you to recall a gene in isolation. They describe a family, a mutation type, or a biopsy and ask you to predict severity, inheritance, or the protein defect, so the mechanism is what must be learned.
prerequisites: Transcription, RNA splicing, the triplet genetic code, and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay

Type I collagen synthesis and post-translational modification

connections.how: RUNX2, SOX9, and HOX genes are the molecular switches behind the ossification and limb patterning events described there.
The Gly-X-Y repeat and hydroxylation steps of collagen synthesis explain why one glycine substitution can cripple the whole triple helix.
Myotonic dystrophy and the dystrophinopathies damage the heart, causing conduction block and dilated cardiomyopathy.
RB1 and TP53 are the model tumor suppressors of the two-hit hypothesis, and EWSR1-FLI1 is a model oncogenic fusion.
Mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS and MERRF affect brain and muscle together because both depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation.

Disproportionate shortening of the proximal limb segments, the humerus and femur.

sections.title: Transcription factors that build the skeleton: RUNX2, SOX9, and HOX genes

blocks.text: Every skeletal cell type arises from mesenchyme, and the choice between becoming a chondrocyte or an osteoblast is made by transcription factors, proteins that bind DNA and switch on whole programs of target genes. Because they sit at the top of these cascades, a modest drop in their dose can change an entire tissue. This explains why many skeletal dysplasias are autosomal dominant through haploinsufficiency rather than through an abnormal protein.
RUNX2 and the osteoblast

RUNX2 (also called CBFA1) is the master regulator of osteoblast differentiation. It commits mesenchymal cells to the osteoblast lineage, induces the downstream factor osterix (SP7), and activates bone matrix genes such as type I collagen and osteocalcin. It is required for both forms of ossification, and in the growth plate it also drives chondrocyte hypertrophy. Mice lacking both copies form a cartilage skeleton with no bone at all.

In humans, losing one copy causes cleidocranial dysplasia, an autosomal dominant disorder. With half the RUNX2 dose, bones that ossify directly from mesenchyme are hit hardest. The clavicles, which ossify largely by the intramembranous route, are hypoplastic or absent, so affected people can bring their shoulders together in front of the chest. The skull vault ossifies late, leaving wide sutures, open fontanelles, and extra (wormian) bones. RUNX2 also acts in the dental lamina, so primary teeth are retained, permanent teeth erupt late, and supernumerary teeth are common. Short stature and delayed ossification of the pubic bones complete the picture.
SOX9 and the chondrocyte

SOX9 is the corresponding switch for cartilage. With SOX5 and SOX6 it turns condensing mesenchyme into chondrocytes and activates type II collagen (COL2A1) and aggrecan. It keeps chondrocytes proliferating and restrains their hypertrophy, opposing RUNX2 within the growth plate. Haploinsufficiency causes campomelic dysplasia, with bowed long bones and a small chest. SOX9 is also required downstream of SRY for Sertoli cell differentiation, so many 46,XY infants with campomelic dysplasia have female or ambiguous genitalia.
HOX genes and segment identity

HOX genes encode homeodomain transcription factors arranged in four clusters (HOXA to HOXD, 39 genes). Genes are expressed along the head to tail axis in the same order as they lie on the chromosome, a property called colinearity, so each segment carries a combinatorial HOX code that tells it what to become. A HOX mutation does not change tissue type; it changes position or identity, for example a vertebra with the form of its neighbor or a cervical rib. In the limb, HOXD13 mutations cause synpolydactyly and HOXA13 mutations cause hand-foot-genital syndrome. Retinoic acid excess shifts HOX expression, which helps explain retinoid embryopathy.

sections.title: Achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain of function and the paternal age effect

blocks.text: Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia causing disproportionate short stature, occurring in about 1 in 25,000 births. It is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) on chromosome 4p. FGFR3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase on growth plate chondrocytes, and its normal role is a brake: when FGF binds, the receptor dimerizes, autophosphorylates, and signals through STAT1 and the MAPK (ERK) pathway to slow chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy.

About 98% of cases carry the same substitution, glycine to arginine at position 380 (G380R) in the transmembrane domain. The mutant receptor signals without enough ligand and escapes normal downregulation, so the brake is pressed constantly. The proliferative and hypertrophic zones of every growth plate are thin, and bones that lengthen through a cartilage model stay short.

blocks.title: From FGFR3 mutation to short limbs
steps: G380R mutation in FGFR3 transmembrane domain

STAT1 and MAPK pathways persistently active
Chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy suppressed
Thin proliferative and hypertrophic zones
Short endochondral bones; membranous bone spared
blocks.caption: The mutation exaggerates a normal growth-limiting signal rather than creating a new function.

blocks.text: The phenotype follows the type of ossification. Long bones are short, worst in the proximal segments (rhizomelia), and the hands are short with a gap between the middle and ring fingers (trident hand). The skull base forms in cartilage, so the foramen magnum is small and can compress the cervicomedullary junction, and a narrow spinal canal can cause stenosis in adults. The skull vault and facial bones grow by membranous ossification and are unaffected, so the head is large with frontal bossing beside a flat midface. The trunk is near normal in length, and intelligence is normal.

The inheritance is autosomal dominant with complete penetrance, but about 80% of affected children are born to parents of average stature, so most cases are new mutations. These arise almost entirely on the paternal allele, and their frequency rises with the father's age. Spermatogonial stem cells divide continuously from puberty onward, giving many replication cycles, and the G380R mutation also gives the spermatogonia that carry it a growth advantage, so mutant clones expand within the testis over time. Oocytes complete their mitotic divisions before birth, so maternal age has no such effect. Homozygosity for the mutation is usually lethal soon after birth, and more severe FGFR3 mutations cause thanatophoric dysplasia.

blocks.predict: Two people with achondroplasia plan a family. What are the outcomes for each pregnancy?
blocks.explain: Each parent passes the mutant allele half the time, so 25% of children are unaffected, 50% are heterozygous with achondroplasia, and 25% are homozygous, a usually lethal severe form.

sections.title: Osteogenesis imperfecta: dominant negative versus null collagen alleles

blocks.text: Type I collagen gives bone, skin, tendon, sclera, dentin, and the ossicles their tensile strength. Each molecule is a triple helix of two pro-alpha-1(I) chains, encoded by COL1A1 on chromosome 17, and one pro-alpha-2(I) chain, encoded by COL1A2 on chromosome 7. Every chain has the repeating sequence Gly-X-Y, where X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline. Glycine has only a hydrogen side chain, and it is the only residue small enough to sit in the crowded center of the helix where the three chains meet. The helix also folds like a zipper from the C-terminal end toward the N-terminal end.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a group of disorders of brittle bone, most of them autosomal dominant mutations in these two genes. The severity depends far more on the type of mutation than on which gene is hit, because what matters is what reaches the triple helix.

A null allele, usually a premature stop codon in COL1A1 that triggers nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, makes no chain at all. Every collagen molecule assembled is normal, but there is only about half as much. This quantitative defect causes OI type I, the mildest and most common form.

A glycine substitution makes a chain that is synthesized and incorporated into helices. The bulky residue blocks the zipper at that point, so folding stalls. While the chains wait unfolded in the endoplasmic reticulum, hydroxylases and glycosyltransferases keep modifying them, and the overmodified molecules are retained, degraded, or secreted as abnormal fibrils that mineralize poorly. Because the mutant chain spoils normal chains that join it, this is a dominant negative effect. Substitutions near the C-terminal end usually disrupt more of the helix and are more severe. These qualitative defects cause types II, III, and IV.

blocks.title: Why a COL1A1 substitution is worse than a null allele
blocks.text: In a COL1A1 glycine substitution, half of all alpha-1 chains are mutant. Each molecule takes two alpha-1 chains at random, so the chance that both are normal is 1/2 times 1/2, or 1/4. Only about one quarter of molecules are normal and three quarters are abnormal. A COL1A2 substitution affects the single alpha-2 chain, so half the molecules are abnormal, which is one reason COL1A2 substitutions are on average milder. A COL1A1 null allele makes only half the alpha-1 chains, so half the usual number of molecules form, but all of them are normal. Half of normal collagen is compatible with mild disease; three quarters abnormal collagen disrupts the whole matrix.

blocks.text: Less often, OI is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in genes for the enzymes and chaperones that modify and fold type I collagen. Because fractures with little trauma raise the question of child abuse, the history, sclerae, teeth, and family pattern matter when interpreting fractures in a child.

sections.title: Dystrophin and the reading frame rule: Duchenne and Becker

blocks.text: Dystrophin is a large cytoskeletal protein on the inner face of the sarcolemma. Its N-terminal end binds actin, a long central rod domain acts as a flexible spacer, and its C-terminal region binds beta-dystroglycan in the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. Through alpha-dystroglycan, which binds laminin in the basement membrane, the complex links the contractile apparatus to the extracellular matrix and spreads the mechanical stress of contraction across the membrane.

blocks.title: From frameshift to muscle loss in Duchenne
steps: Out-of-frame deletion in DMD
Premature stop codon downstream
Nonsense-mediated decay; no dystrophin
Sarcolemma tears during contraction
Ca2+ influx, protease activation, fiber necrosis
Regeneration fails; fat and fibrous tissue replace muscle
blocks.caption: Creatine kinase leaks from damaged fibers and is markedly elevated from early childhood.

blocks.text: The DMD gene at Xp21 is the largest known human gene, about 2.2 million base pairs with 79 exons. About two thirds of mutations are exon deletions clustered in a central hot spot; most others are duplications and point mutations. Disease severity is predicted by the reading frame rule, which holds in about 90% of cases. Ribosomes read mRNA in consecutive triplets from the start codon. If the deletion removes a number of coding nucleotides that is not a multiple of three, every downstream codon is misread and a premature stop codon soon appears, so no functional dystrophin is made. This is Duchenne muscular dystrophy. If the number is a multiple of three, the frame is preserved: a shorter protein lacking part of the rod domain is made, but it keeps the actin-binding and dystroglycan-binding ends and works partly. This is Becker muscular dystrophy.

blocks.title: Applying the reading frame rule
blocks.text: Boy A has a deletion removing 1,000 coding nucleotides; boy B has one removing 3,600. Divide by three. For A, 1,000 / 3 = 333 with a remainder of 1, so the frame shifts by one nucleotide, a stop codon follows, and no dystrophin is made: Duchenne. For B, 3,600 / 3 = 1,200 exactly, so 1,200 amino acids are lost from the rod domain but the frame and both functional ends are kept: Becker, despite the larger deletion. The rule uses nucleotides in the mature mRNA, so a whole-exon deletion keeps the frame only when the exons on either side join in phase.

blocks.title: Duchenne and Becker compared
rows: Early childhood, usually by about 5 years
Loss of walking by early teens; death from respiratory or cardiac failure, often in the 20s or 30s
Proximal weakness, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, high CK, dilated cardiomyopathy
Same pattern, milder; cardiomyopathy may dominate
blocks.caption: Both are X-linked recessive and both involve the heart; the difference lies in how much working dystrophin is made.

blocks.text: Gowers sign, pushing on the thighs to stand from the floor, reflects pelvic girdle weakness. Calf pseudohypertrophy is enlargement from fat and connective tissue replacing muscle, not true hypertrophy. Female carriers are usually unaffected, but skewed X inactivation can produce manifesting carriers with weakness or cardiomyopathy.

Duchenne affects about 1 in 3,500 to 5,000 male births, and about one third of cases are new mutations. The huge gene is a large target, so its mutation rate per generation is among the highest known, and affected males rarely reproduce, so each lost allele must be replaced by new mutation to keep the frequency steady; for an X-linked lethal disorder the expected share of new cases at equilibrium is about one third. Mothers of an isolated case may also carry germline mosaicism, so recurrence risk is not zero even when maternal blood testing is normal.

sections.title: Myotonic dystrophy type 1: CTG repeat expansion and toxic RNA

blocks.text: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is the most common muscular dystrophy beginning in adulthood. It is autosomal dominant and caused by expansion of a CTG trinucleotide repeat in the 3' untranslated region of the DMPK gene on chromosome 19q. Normal alleles carry about 5 to 34 repeats, alleles of about 35 to 49 are unstable but cause no symptoms, and about 50 or more cause disease. Larger expansions give earlier onset and more severe disease.

Because the repeat lies outside the coding sequence, the main problem is not a missing DMPK protein but the RNA itself, a toxic RNA gain of function. The expanded CUG repeat folds into hairpins that stay in the nucleus as foci and trap the splicing regulator muscleblind-like 1 (MBNL1), while another regulator, CELF1, becomes overactive. Many transcripts then revert to fetal splice forms, and the protein products work poorly in adult tissue. This one mechanism explains why the disease reaches muscle, heart, lens, testis, and endocrine tissue at once.

blocks.text: Myotonia is delayed relaxation after voluntary contraction, seen as a slow release of a handgrip or a sustained dimple after percussion of the thenar eminence. It arises because mis-splicing of the skeletal muscle chloride channel ClC-1 lowers chloride conductance, which normally provides most of the resting conductance of the fiber. Without that stabilizing current, K+ that accumulates in the T-tubules during activity depolarizes the membrane, and the fiber keeps firing after the nerve stops.

Posterior subcapsular cataracts, often early and iridescent
Mis-splicing toward the less active fetal insulin receptor isoform
blocks.caption: Distal weakness with myotonia, cataracts, and a conduction defect is the classic DM1 pattern.

blocks.text: The repeat is unstable in meiosis and tends to grow from parent to child, so onset becomes earlier and disease more severe in later generations. This is anticipation. The largest expansions, often over 1,000 repeats, arise almost entirely in the female germline, so congenital DM1, with severe hypotonia, respiratory failure, feeding difficulty, and intellectual disability, is nearly always inherited from the mother, who may be mildly affected and unaware of her diagnosis. Myotonic dystrophy type 2, a CCTG expansion in CNBP, is milder, mainly proximal, and shows no congenital form.

blocks.predict: A floppy newborn needs ventilation, and testing shows a very large CTG expansion in DMPK. Which parent most likely transmitted it, and what might you find on examining that parent?
blocks.explain: The mother. Massive expansions arise mainly in female meiosis. She may have mild myotonia, distal hand weakness, early cataracts, or a prolonged PR interval she has never had evaluated.

sections.title: Mitochondrial myopathies: maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, and ragged red fibers

blocks.text: Each mitochondrion carries several copies of a small circular DNA of about 16,600 base pairs. It encodes 37 genes: 13 polypeptides of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, 22 transfer RNAs, and 2 ribosomal RNAs. All other mitochondrial proteins, including most respiratory chain subunits, are nuclear encoded. A mutation in an mtDNA tRNA gene impairs translation of all 13 mtDNA-encoded proteins, so ATP production fails broadly.

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother. The oocyte contributes hundreds of thousands of mtDNA copies, while the few sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilization. An affected mother can therefore pass the disorder to all her children of either sex, and an affected father passes it to none.

Heteroplasmy explains why that transmission is so variable. Cells contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA, and at each cell division mitochondria are distributed to daughter cells at random, so the proportion drifts between cell lines and tissues. During oogenesis only a small number of mtDNA molecules populate each developing egg, a genetic bottleneck, so siblings can inherit very different mutant loads from the same mother. Disease appears in a tissue only when the mutant fraction exceeds its threshold, and tissues with the highest dependence on oxidative phosphorylation, skeletal muscle, brain, heart, retina, and cochlea, cross it first. With oxidative phosphorylation blocked, NADH accumulates and pyruvate is converted to lactate, producing lactic acidosis that worsens with exercise.

blocks.title: Mitochondrial inheritance compared with Mendelian patterns
rows: Carrier mother to sons; no father to son transmission
Mother to all children; never through the father

blocks.caption: Many respiratory chain disorders are caused by nuclear genes and follow Mendelian rules; only mtDNA mutations show maternal inheritance.

blocks.text: The muscle biopsy shows the compensation. Muscle fibers that cannot make ATP proliferate mitochondria, which collect beneath the sarcolemma. With the modified Gomori trichrome stain these subsarcolemmal clumps stain red against blue-green myofibrils, giving the irregular ragged red fiber. Electron microscopy shows enlarged mitochondria with abnormal cristae and paracrystalline inclusions. Ragged red fibers point to a mitochondrial disorder but are not specific to one syndrome.

sections.title: Genetics of bone and soft tissue sarcomas: RB1, TP53, and EWSR1-FLI1

blocks.text: Sarcomas show the two main routes to cancer. Tumor suppressor genes cause disease through loss of function, so both alleles must be inactivated in a cell. Oncogenes cause disease through gain of function, so one altered allele is enough. Both RB1 and TP53 guard the G1 to S transition, which is why their loss is so common in osteosarcoma, a tumor of rapidly dividing bone-forming cells.
RB1 and osteosarcoma

The RB protein, encoded by RB1 on chromosome 13q14, holds cells in G1. When hypophosphorylated, it binds the transcription factor E2F and blocks transcription of the genes needed for DNA synthesis. Growth signals raise cyclin D, and cyclin D with CDK4 or CDK6 phosphorylates RB, which releases E2F and lets the cell enter S phase. Without RB, the checkpoint is open permanently.

blocks.title: RB control of the G1 to S checkpoint
steps: Hypophosphorylated RB binds E2F; cell held in G1
Growth signals raise cyclin D
Cyclin D with CDK4 or CDK6 phosphorylates RB
E2F released; S phase genes transcribed
Cell divides; RB dephosphorylated in the next G1
blocks.caption: Loss of RB, or of CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p16, removes this brake.

blocks.text: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis came from retinoblastoma. In the hereditary form, a germline RB1 mutation is present in every cell, so only one somatic hit, often loss of heterozygosity, is needed. Tumors appear earlier, are often bilateral, and recur in other tissues: survivors have a markedly increased risk of osteosarcoma in adolescence, both within and outside radiation fields, and of soft tissue sarcomas and melanoma. Predisposition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait even though the gene acts recessively in each cell.
TP53 and Li-Fraumeni syndrome

p53, encoded by TP53 on 17p13, senses DNA damage. Normally MDM2 keeps it low by targeting it for degradation; damage activates ATM and ATR kinases, which stabilize p53. p53 then induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that blocks RB phosphorylation and arrests the cell in G1 for repair, or triggers apoptosis through BAX and related proteins when damage is beyond repair. A germline TP53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition with a very high lifetime cancer risk at young ages: soft tissue sarcoma and osteosarcoma, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma, and leukemia. Several different early cancers in one family suggest the diagnosis.
EWSR1-FLI1 and Ewing sarcoma

Ewing sarcoma is driven instead by a gain of function. In about 85% of cases the translocation t(11;22)(q24;q12) joins the 5' part of EWSR1 on chromosome 22 to the 3' part of FLI1 on chromosome 11. The fusion protein combines the strong transactivation domain of EWS with the ETS DNA-binding domain of FLI1, making an abnormal transcription factor that binds GGAA microsatellite repeats and switches on a growth program while repressing differentiation genes. A smaller share of tumors carry other EWSR1 fusions, such as EWSR1-ERG.

integration.text: The common thread is that the type of mutation predicts the disease better than the name of the gene. Loss of one copy of a dose-sensitive transcription factor (RUNX2, SOX9) gives haploinsufficiency. Overactivity of a growth-limiting receptor (FGFR3) gives a dominant gain of function. An abnormal subunit of a multimeric structure (collagen) gives a dominant negative effect that is worse than having no subunit at all. In dystrophin the reading frame, not deletion size, decides whether any protein is made. In DM1 the gene product barely matters because the RNA itself is toxic, and in mitochondrial disease the dose of mutant DNA varies cell by cell. Sarcomas repeat the pattern at the level of the cell: tumor suppressors need two hits, while a fusion oncogene needs one event.

These mechanisms link anatomy, biochemistry, and pathology. Membranous versus endochondral ossification explains which bones suffer in cleidocranial dysplasia and achondroplasia; collagen folding explains OI; membrane mechanics and Ca2+ entry explain dystrophic necrosis; splicing and ion channel physiology explain myotonia; and oxidative phosphorylation explains lactic acidosis and ragged red fibers. The limits matter too: the reading frame rule has exceptions, heteroplasmy measured in blood may not reflect muscle, and the same syndrome can arise from several genes, so a phenotype points to a mechanism before it points to a single mutation.

summary: RUNX2 drives osteoblast differentiation; its haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia with absent clavicles, open fontanelles, delayed suture closure, and extra teeth.
SOX9 drives chondrocyte differentiation (campomelic dysplasia, often with 46,XY sex reversal), and HOX genes assign segment identity in colinear order.
Achondroplasia is FGFR3 gain of function (usually G380R) that suppresses growth plate chondrocytes; endochondral bone is short while membranous bone is spared.
About 80% of achondroplasia is new mutation on the paternal allele, rising with paternal age through continuous spermatogonial division and clonal advantage.
In OI, a glycine substitution acts dominant negatively (only about 1 in 4 molecules normal with COL1A1), causing types II to IV; a null allele halves normal collagen, causing mild type I.
Out-of-frame DMD deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame deletions leave a shortened, partly functional protein (Becker), whatever the deletion size.
The DMD gene is the largest human gene, so its mutation rate is high and about one third of Duchenne cases are new mutations.

DM1 is an autosomal dominant CTG expansion in DMPK whose toxic RNA disrupts splicing, causing myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, balding, testicular atrophy, and conduction block, with maternal transmission of the congenital form.

mtDNA disorders pass only from mother to children; heteroplasmy, the oocyte bottleneck, and tissue thresholds make severity vary, and ragged red fibers appear on modified Gomori trichrome in MERRF and MELAS.
Germline RB1 loss raises osteosarcoma risk, germline TP53 loss causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and t(11;22) creates the EWSR1-FLI1 transcription factor of Ewing sarcoma.

verify: Incidence figures (achondroplasia about 1 in 25,000; Duchenne about 1 in 3,500 to 5,000 male births) vary among sources; confirm the values NABNE uses if tested.
DM1 repeat thresholds (normal about 5 to 34, unstable 35 to 49, affected 50 or more, congenital often over 1,000) follow current genetic references; older texts give slightly different cutoffs.

The proportions quoted for the G380R FGFR3 mutation (about 98%), DMD deletions (about two thirds), the reading frame rule (about 90%), t(11;22) in Ewing sarcoma (about 85%), and the common MERRF and MELAS point mutations (about 80% each) are approximate consensus values.
OI classification has been expanded beyond Sillence types I to IV to include recessive types from collagen-processing genes; confirm whether NABNE expects only types I to IV.

Recurrence risk for unaffected parents of a child with de novo achondroplasia, and the rate of maternal germline mosaicism in isolated Duchenne cases, are given differently across sources and were left unquantified here.

Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Gowers sign, Codman triangle, and Knudson two-hit hypothesis, and the gene names CBFA1, osterix, MBNL1, and CELF1, or only the core genes named in the competencies.
